summary: We are testing whether a skyline-based greedy 2D packer dramatically outperforms naive 1D strip packing for the polyomino rectangle-minimization problem. Two arms will run: the main arm (skyline packer with multi-width sweep) predicted to score ~76, and a negative control (strip packer) predicted to score ~34, with scores measured via the judge's continuous 0-100 metric (score = 1e5·Σkᵢ / A).
key_points: Main arm: Skyline greedy packer generates all orientations (reflect+rotate) per piece, sorts pieces by decreasing size, and for ~160 candidate widths places each piece at the skyline position minimizing max height. Predicted score ~76 based on probe runs.

Negative control: Naive strip packer places pieces left-to-right in a single row with no vertical compaction, yielding predicted score ~34. This validates the measurement pipeline and quantifies how much the 2D skyline mechanism contributes.

Confirmation criterion: If the skyline arm scores ≥70 and the strip arm scores ≤40, the hypothesis is confirmed — the ~2× score gap demonstrates that exploiting 2D spatial gaps (skyline) is the dominant mechanism for packing quality. Refutation: if both arms score similarly (<10 point gap), the skyline mechanism provides negligible benefit at this problem scale.

Key risks: (1) Transform parameter bugs (X,Y,R,F) could cause checker rejection → score 0, (2) time budget pressure on large n=10000 cases with 160-width sweep, (3) piece ordering sensitivity not yet characterized. Diagnostics are specified for each failure mode.
